medical.title: Nerve signaling pathway reveals how a tuberculosis molecule triggers cough
medical.summary: A molecule produced by some highly transmissible strains of tuberculosis (TB) bacteria activates sensory nerves and triggers coughing, according to a study led by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers. The findings, published in Nature Microbiology, uncover a signaling pathway that could be targeted with drugs developed for chronic cough, offering a possible approach to relieving TB-associated cough and reducing transmission.

medical.title: Molecular backdoor destroys 'undruggable' protein driving rare childhood cancer
medical.summary: A secret molecular backdoor let researchers from Penn State College of Medicine destroy a protein that drives a rare and often fatal bone and soft tissue cancer in children and adolescents that often returns in treatment-resistant forms. Now, just three years after the discovery, a Phase I clinical trial is underway and, once complete, a Phase II trial to test the approach's efficacy in patients will follow shortly thereafter.

medical.title: How brain aging differs from neurodegeneration: New data could help in the search for dementia drugs
medical.summary: Researchers from Skoltech, together with colleagues from Ben-Gurion University (Israel) and other organizations, studied how the spatial organization of DNA in neurons changes during natural aging and in the development of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's. The results showed that, although chromatin regulation is disrupted during aging, the onset of neurodegenerative diseases is driven by an additional factor—the accumulation of DNA damage.

medical.title: Salt reduction could maximize kidney drug benefits
medical.summary: Reducing salt intake to guideline-recommended levels could substantially enhance the kidney-protective effects of an emerging class of treatments for chronic kidney disease, a study suggests.

medical.title: How the intestine keeps its tremendous surface area in order
medical.summary: The small intestine is constantly in flux. This 20-foot-long (6.1-meter-long) tube is lined with structures that absorb the nutrients during digestion. The cells at the tip of these structures are continuously replaced, but how they stay organized has not been well understood.

medical.title: Dual inhibition of transcriptional kinases and anti-apoptotic proteins targets tumor growth
medical.summary: In cancer research, the protein kinases CDK12 and CDK13 are attracting attention as promising targets for therapy. These enzymes regulate gene transcription by phosphorylating—transferring a phosphate group to—the protein complex RNA polymerase II, which transcribes DNA. Inhibiting CDK12 and CDK13 disrupts the transcription of particularly long genes, which leads to defects in DNA damage repair and thus the suppression of cancer cell proliferation.

medical.title: Court-appointed medical guardian study reveals role in care of highly vulnerable older adults
medical.summary: When University of Michigan Health geriatrician Kahli Zietlow, M.D., gets summoned to the hospital room of a seriously ill older adult, she knows the assessments she performs might help determine if the patient can make their own medical decisions or if someone else will have to. But if the patient's health or mental capacity has declined too far before they could legally authorize someone to make medical decisions for them, then Zietlow knows that the hospital may ask a probate court to assign a guardian to make those decisions, either temporarily or permanently.

medical.title: AI-powered lifestyle modification chatbot offers advice, accountability, affordability
medical.summary: Many of the 79% of American adults trying to improve their diet and exercise habits seek guidance. But personal coaches are expensive, and self-help lifestyle apps, while affordable, lack accountability.

medical.title: Lung complications affect 1 in 3 patients receiving antibody-drug conjugates for lung cancer, study finds
medical.summary: A study led by The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center—Arthur G. James Cancer Hospital and Richard J. Solove Research Institute (OSUCCC—James) sheds light on safety concerns as antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) become more important in lung cancer treatment. The findings highlight the need to catch and manage side effects like lung toxicity much earlier to help patients safely benefit from ADCs.

medical.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
medical.summary: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

medical.title: Single vaping episode impairs vascular function, study finds
medical.summary: Researchers have identified acute negative effects of vaping, even without nicotine, on vascular function. The results of the study are being presented next week at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA).

medical.title: Elevated blood sugar levels over decades linked to worse midlife memory and cognitive function
medical.summary: Young adults with a progressive rise in fasting blood sugar levels over multiple decades were more likely to have worse cognitive health by midlife. Participants who developed type 2 diabetes during the study also had signs of structural brain changes, according to new, independent research published in the Journal of the American Heart Association.

medical.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
medical.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

medical.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
medical.summary: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

medical.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
medical.summary: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

science.title: Functional traits in two Asian pines covary with climate and genomic ancestry
science.summary: Wood and needle traits in two closely related pines in southern Yunnan covary with climate and genomic ancestry, according to a new study published in Plant Diversity. Wood anatomical traits were more strongly associated with climate, while needle traits were linked to both climate and parental ancestry.

science.title: South Pole Telescope releases clearest map ever of matter in the distant universe
science.summary: The earliest light in the universe, known as the cosmic microwave background (CMB), has been traveling since the dawn of the universe more than 14 billion years ago. A group of scientists from 30 institutions has now released the sharpest and clearest map ever made of the mass in the universe, created by measuring how this ancient light was bent as it traveled.

science.title: Ban AI, lose Google Search: Schools face tough choice over students' access
science.summary: Three major school districts in the United States are contemplating moving away from Google search engines, so students are not forced to use artificial intelligence (AI) in their daily schoolwork.

science.title: Webb discovers farthest 'little red dot' from universe's first 500 million years
science.summary: Following the discovery of faint supermassive black holes called little red dots (LRDs) in the early universe in 2022, an international team of researchers has found the farthest little red dot to date, reports a new study in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

science.title: Who identifies as a prepper? New study offers surprising answers
science.summary: Amid rising concerns about natural disasters, geopolitical instability, public health threats and emerging technologies, new research on who identifies as a "prepper" in the United States shows that the group is larger and more diverse than previously thought.

science.title: New PET tracer cocktail rapidly detects hospital-acquired bacterial infections
science.summary: A novel radiotracer cocktail can accurately identify multiple strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa—a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections—within hours, according to new research published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine. By targeting multiple strains of the bacteria, this rapid detection approach has the potential to enable targeted therapy and reduce the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics among critically ill patients.

science.title: Amber fossils reveal how grasshoppers may have walked on water 100 million years ago
science.summary: Walking on water represents one of the most striking modes of locomotion in the natural world and plays a crucial role in animals' colonization of ecological niches at the water surface. However, insects specialized for this locomotion (obligate surface dwellers) belong to only two groups: the living Gerromorpha (Hemiptera) and extinct Chresmodidae (stem group of Polyneoptera). Elucidating how extinct insects moved on the water surface has proven highly challenging, and the adaptive evolution of different insect lineages to ecological niches at the water surface remains poorly understood.

science.title: New measurements suggest surrounding liquids control water layer formation on submerged ice
science.summary: The behavior of ice exposed to a vacuum or vapor has been studied extensively, but ice submerged in a liquid is more difficult to study. Temperature changes cause the ice to dissolve or grow, resulting in fluctuating interfaces.

science.title: Most precise measurement of coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering to date tightens limits on new forces
science.summary: Neutrinos are tiny elementary particles with little mass and no electric charge. While most neutrinos pass through matter without interacting, a neutrino can occasionally scatter off an atomic nucleus, transferring a little energy to it and causing it to move.

science.title: Successful AI integration in manufacturing hinges on employees' attitudes to AI
science.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) has grown more capable, industries across China are adopting AI to improve productivity and capability. One such industry is the textile and clothing industry, which has historically been very labor-intensive.

science.title: Genetic analysis reveals peak orchid root fungal diversity at one of the most biodiverse places on Earth
science.summary: The fungal communities living in the roots of epiphytic orchids vary with altitude, location and orchid species, according to research published in the journal Microbial Ecology. The study, conducted in Podocarpus National Park in southern Ecuador, found that mid-elevation forests harbor the greatest diversity of these microorganisms, while their richness decreases at higher elevations and their community composition differs.

science.title: How utilities, communities can help build resilience for vulnerable families during power outages
science.summary: For low-income households, extended power outages can create devastating losses of food and money, as well as feelings of comfort and security within their homes, according to research led by the University of Michigan.

science.title: Board diversity and digital readiness linked to corporate adaptability during pandemic
science.summary: Think "pandemic" and the word "pivot" is not far behind. What happened to organizational communications during COVID-19, though, was an unprecedented sea change. For businesses trying to stay connected to investors like pension and mutual funds, in-person roadshows, brokerage-hosted conferences and "analyst day" meetings were adapted into virtual versions filtered through the safety of personal digital devices as everyone hunkered down at home.

science.title: Japan unveils rover prototype for moon water mission
science.summary: Japan's space agency unveiled Wednesday a test model of a rover that will travel to the moon's south pole in a search for water, which could potentially be used for rocket fuel.

science.title: China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying 2 Chinese and 1 Pakistani astronaut
science.summary: China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts—two Chinese and a Pakistani—sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.

science.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
science.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

science.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
science.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

science.title: Not everything that sounds plausible works: Testing ideas to win support for carbon pricing
science.summary: What makes people support a carbon price? To find out, 108 researchers, led by a research team at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, tested 55 different ideas at the same time, from information campaigns to reflection tasks. On average, there was a small but statistically significant positive effect. Individually, the effect was detectable for only 11 of the 55 ideas. One of the strongest effects came from writing a letter to a fictional person of a future generation. The results were recently published in the journal Nature Human Behaviour.

science.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
science.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

science.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
science.summary: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
environment.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
environment.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
environment.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: How the intestine keeps its tremendous surface area in order
mix_items.summary: The small intestine is constantly in flux. This 20-foot-long (6.1-meter-long) tube is lined with structures that absorb the nutrients during digestion. The cells at the tip of these structures are continuously replaced, but how they stay organized has not been well understood.

mix_items.title: De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze
mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: New PET tracer cocktail rapidly detects hospital-acquired bacterial infections
mix_items.summary: A novel radiotracer cocktail can accurately identify multiple strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa—a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections—within hours, according to new research published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine. By targeting multiple strains of the bacteria, this rapid detection approach has the potential to enable targeted therapy and reduce the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics among critically ill patients.

mix_items.title: Dual inhibition of transcriptional kinases and anti-apoptotic proteins targets tumor growth
mix_items.summary: In cancer research, the protein kinases CDK12 and CDK13 are attracting attention as promising targets for therapy. These enzymes regulate gene transcription by phosphorylating—transferring a phosphate group to—the protein complex RNA polymerase II, which transcribes DNA. Inhibiting CDK12 and CDK13 disrupts the transcription of particularly long genes, which leads to defects in DNA damage repair and thus the suppression of cancer cell proliferation.

mix_items.title: Amber fossils reveal how grasshoppers may have walked on water 100 million years ago
mix_items.summary: Walking on water represents one of the most striking modes of locomotion in the natural world and plays a crucial role in animals' colonization of ecological niches at the water surface. However, insects specialized for this locomotion (obligate surface dwellers) belong to only two groups: the living Gerromorpha (Hemiptera) and extinct Chresmodidae (stem group of Polyneoptera). Elucidating how extinct insects moved on the water surface has proven highly challenging, and the adaptive evolution of different insect lineages to ecological niches at the water surface remains poorly understood.

mix_items.title: New measurements suggest surrounding liquids control water layer formation on submerged ice
mix_items.summary: The behavior of ice exposed to a vacuum or vapor has been studied extensively, but ice submerged in a liquid is more difficult to study. Temperature changes cause the ice to dissolve or grow, resulting in fluctuating interfaces.

mix_items.title: Most precise measurement of coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering to date tightens limits on new forces
mix_items.summary: Neutrinos are tiny elementary particles with little mass and no electric charge. While most neutrinos pass through matter without interacting, a neutrino can occasionally scatter off an atomic nucleus, transferring a little energy to it and causing it to move.

mix_items.title: Successful AI integration in manufacturing hinges on employees' attitudes to AI
mix_items.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) has grown more capable, industries across China are adopting AI to improve productivity and capability. One such industry is the textile and clothing industry, which has historically been very labor-intensive.

mix_items.title: Court-appointed medical guardian study reveals role in care of highly vulnerable older adults
mix_items.summary: When University of Michigan Health geriatrician Kahli Zietlow, M.D., gets summoned to the hospital room of a seriously ill older adult, she knows the assessments she performs might help determine if the patient can make their own medical decisions or if someone else will have to. But if the patient's health or mental capacity has declined too far before they could legally authorize someone to make medical decisions for them, then Zietlow knows that the hospital may ask a probate court to assign a guardian to make those decisions, either temporarily or permanently.

mix_items.title: Genetic analysis reveals peak orchid root fungal diversity at one of the most biodiverse places on Earth
mix_items.summary: The fungal communities living in the roots of epiphytic orchids vary with altitude, location and orchid species, according to research published in the journal Microbial Ecology. The study, conducted in Podocarpus National Park in southern Ecuador, found that mid-elevation forests harbor the greatest diversity of these microorganisms, while their richness decreases at higher elevations and their community composition differs.

mix_items.title: AI-powered lifestyle modification chatbot offers advice, accountability, affordability
mix_items.summary: Many of the 79% of American adults trying to improve their diet and exercise habits seek guidance. But personal coaches are expensive, and self-help lifestyle apps, while affordable, lack accountability.

mix_items.title: How utilities, communities can help build resilience for vulnerable families during power outages
mix_items.summary: For low-income households, extended power outages can create devastating losses of food and money, as well as feelings of comfort and security within their homes, according to research led by the University of Michigan.

mix_items.title: Board diversity and digital readiness linked to corporate adaptability during pandemic
mix_items.summary: Think "pandemic" and the word "pivot" is not far behind. What happened to organizational communications during COVID-19, though, was an unprecedented sea change. For businesses trying to stay connected to investors like pension and mutual funds, in-person roadshows, brokerage-hosted conferences and "analyst day" meetings were adapted into virtual versions filtered through the safety of personal digital devices as everyone hunkered down at home.

mix_items.title: Lung complications affect 1 in 3 patients receiving antibody-drug conjugates for lung cancer, study finds
mix_items.summary: A study led by The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center—Arthur G. James Cancer Hospital and Richard J. Solove Research Institute (OSUCCC—James) sheds light on safety concerns as antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) become more important in lung cancer treatment. The findings highlight the need to catch and manage side effects like lung toxicity much earlier to help patients safely benefit from ADCs.

mix_items.title: Japan unveils rover prototype for moon water mission
mix_items.summary: Japan's space agency unveiled Wednesday a test model of a rover that will travel to the moon's south pole in a search for water, which could potentially be used for rocket fuel.

mix_items.title: China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying 2 Chinese and 1 Pakistani astronaut
mix_items.summary: China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts—two Chinese and a Pakistani—sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.

mix_items.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
mix_items.summary: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

mix_items.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
mix_items.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

mix_items.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
mix_items.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

mix_items.title: Single vaping episode impairs vascular function, study finds
mix_items.summary: Researchers have identified acute negative effects of vaping, even without nicotine, on vascular function. The results of the study are being presented next week at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA).

mix_items.title: Elevated blood sugar levels over decades linked to worse midlife memory and cognitive function
mix_items.summary: Young adults with a progressive rise in fasting blood sugar levels over multiple decades were more likely to have worse cognitive health by midlife. Participants who developed type 2 diabetes during the study also had signs of structural brain changes, according to new, independent research published in the Journal of the American Heart Association.

mix_items.title: Not everything that sounds plausible works: Testing ideas to win support for carbon pricing
mix_items.summary: What makes people support a carbon price? To find out, 108 researchers, led by a research team at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, tested 55 different ideas at the same time, from information campaigns to reflection tasks. On average, there was a small but statistically significant positive effect. Individually, the effect was detectable for only 11 of the 55 ideas. One of the strongest effects came from writing a letter to a fictional person of a future generation. The results were recently published in the journal Nature Human Behaviour.

mix_items.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
mix_items.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

mix_items.title: Georgia’s Pecan Belt
mix_items.summary: Since an early-1900s planting boom, orchards along the Flint River in southwest Georgia have become a center of U.S. pecan production.

mix_items.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
mix_items.summary: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

mix_items.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
mix_items.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

mix_items.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
mix_items.summary: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
mix_items.summary: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

mix_items.title: Ecuador’s bioeconomy plan vows sustainability, but faces a test of government priorities
mix_items.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. It aims to innovate agribusiness, ecotourism, and other industries in rural areas, without threatening the environment or Indigenous communities. The National […]

mix_items.title: As new season starts, Antarctic krill-fishing vessels face urgent conservation decision (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Despite promising developments, the 27 member states of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) have again failed to reach an agreement that protects the Southern Ocean. Mired by consensus decision-making and shrouded from public view by confidentiality rules, Antarctica’s governance systems are no longer fulfilling their mandate. This leaves room […]

mix_items.summary: The bare ridges of the Tunari mountain range rise high in Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department. Only the occasional stand of squat, shrubby trees and rust-red potato crops dot the slopes. It wasn’t always this way. The high-elevation landscape was once filled with native Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) trees, a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family […]

mix_items.summary: ANATALYA, Türkiye — A year ago, a record number of Indigenous people attended the United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil. Although there as observers, without a seat at the negotiating table, they left with promises: recognition of their lands, a share of a new forest fund, and a just transition mechanism in the making. mix_items.summary: EDINBURGH — Ocean conservation efforts are being hindered by inadequate funding, as well as difficulties translating research into action, according to attendees of an international marine conservation congress in Scotland. mix_items.title: Indonesia fires test palm oil certification scheme as NGOs question RSPO accountability
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Environmental groups are questioning the effectiveness of a global organization that develops standards and certification for sustainable palm oil production after fires affected thousands of hectares in concessions belonging to its members in Indonesia — including areas certified under its sustainability scheme. The criticism came as the organization, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm […]

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
